newsitem.title: UK: Gasoline seen facing MTBE price pressure in August.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline seen facing MTBE price pressure in August.

text.p: Prices for high octane gasoline traded in the Atlantic basin will continue to face upward pressure from methyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE), a key gasoline component, at least through to second half August, European MTBE marketers said Friday.

No further MTBE price gains are expected, but while some major European producers and traders expect prices on both sides of the Atlantic to begin falling by second half August, others see no significant declines before September or potentially the third quarter.

"The supply situation in Europe will remain tight for another couple of weeks, but from the middle of August we expect levels to come down on increased availability," a major trans-Atlantic producers said.
He predicted MTBE prices, currently quoted around $315 a tonne FOB Rotterdam, would stay well above $300 until mid-August before falling back decisively thereafter.

A leading European MTBE and reformulated gasoline marketer, however, said continuing production problems at world-scale plants in Venezuela and Saudi Arabia would keep the MTBE market tight and values high "for some time to come."
"I don't expect prices to go down as quickly as they came up," he commented, implying that no major erosion would likely be seen during the course of August.
A third important supplier, based in the Benelux, was more bullish still.

Predicting demand for gasoline, and by implication, MTBE, to remain high and perhaps even rise further, especially in the U.S., through August, the player said it was conceivable that no major change would be seen before the fourth quarter.
A string of U.S. and European MTBE production problems and outages during second half June pushed European prices up from around $270 in mid-June to $295-$300 by the start of July.

Despite the resolution of most of those problems during July, an upsurge in trans-Atlantic gasoline demand and prices in a late start to this year's U.S. driving season supported a further $20-$30 rise in MTBE values by the first half of this week.

By Thursday/Friday, MTBE was talked around a reported $314 deal level of Thursday, down from close to $320 mid-week, although European producers insisted they would not part with their scarce volumes below $320 FOB Rotterdam.
These high values and the lack of MTBE have helped in Europe and the U.S. to keep the premium of high octane gasolines over standard grades well above normal levels.
An indicator of MTBE strength against gasoline is the MTBE factor to premium unleaded, which has stayed around or above 1.60 for several weeks compared with a more usual average of 1.40.

The $320 FOB Rotterdam level is the current calculated netback for arb volumes to the U.S. Gulf, which sellers say points to a narrow enough arb to ensure the U.S. will continue dominate MTBE price movements in the near term.
"If the U.S. price now suddenly falls by $20, then so will Europe," a major producer said.
He said the market could expect to see a far greater fall in U.S. gasoline/MTBE values than in Europe "because history shows the U.S. market is simply more volatile."
This would suggest, he contended, that the ARA arb to the U.S. Gulf could close just as European availability increases during the latter part of August or early September.
While others dispute predictions of an early slump in U.S. levels, most agree that European availabilities will significantly improve in September.
"All European plants are back up and running at full capacity, but supply volumes are committed through virtually the whole of August," one marketer said.
Another pointed to reports of a continuing outage at the 12,500 barrels per day (500,000 tonnes a year) Superoctanos MTBE plant in Jose, Venezuela, as an indicator of persistent bottlenecks.
A Scandinavian marketer meanwhile said the 700,000 tonnes a year Shell/Sabic (Sadaf) plant in Al Jubail, Saudi Arabia, was still running well below capacity after recent problems.
